\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related_work}

Document-level relation extraction (DocRE) requires reasoning across sentence boundaries to identify relations between entity pairs.
DocRED \citep{yao2019docred} established the first large-scale benchmark for this task, catalyzing a line of encoder-based methods that treat DocRE as classification over entity pair representations.
ATLOP \citep{zhou2021atlop} introduced adaptive thresholding for multi-label prediction and localized context pooling for entity representations.
A parallel thread incorporates sentence-level evidence into these architectures.
SAIS \citep{xiao2022sais} introduced evidence supervision as an auxiliary training signal and showed that joint evidence prediction improves extraction through data augmentation and ensemble inference.
DREEAM \citep{ma2023dreeam} extended this approach with dynamic memory-based evidence retrieval that guides attention to supporting sentences.
EIDER \citep{xie2022eider} jointly trains an evidence extractor and fuses evidence representations into the relation classifier.
In all three systems, evidence identification is binary sentence classification over a fixed candidate set, a formulation that adds no output complexity.
Recent work has recast DocRE for large language models.
AutoRE \citep{autore2024} fine-tunes LLMs with QLoRA using a relation-head-facts decomposition; \citet{xu2024lmrc} frame extraction as multi-choice reading comprehension; RelPrior \citep{wang2025relprior} uses relation priors to guide LLM-based extraction; GLiDRE \citep{zhang2025glidre} presents a generalist lightweight approach; Ru-LLM \citep{wang2025rullm} incorporates logical rule constraints; and \citet{chen2025docksrag} combine retrieval-augmented generation with structured knowledge.
These methods match or surpass encoder baselines but produce bare triplets without evidence.
The critical distinction lies in computational nature: in SAIS and DREEAM, evidence retrieval is classification that regularizes the encoder without increasing output length; in LLM-based DocRE, evidence requires additional output tokens per triple, imposing costs that depend on model capacity and optimization strategy.
Whether this cost is inevitable or can be mitigated is the central question of our work.

Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO; \citealt{shao2024deepseekmath}) eliminates the separate value network by computing advantages within groups.
Subsequent work addresses failure modes: DAPO \citep{yu2025dapo} prevents entropy collapse, Dr.\ GRPO \citep{liu2025drgrpo} corrects length bias, and multi-objective variants \citep{liu2026gdpo,ito2025mogrpo} handle competing reward signals.
Applications to structured IE include R1-RE \citep{dai2025r1re} and REAR \citep{wang2025rear}.
Direct Preference Optimization \citep{rafailov2023direct} reformulates RLHF as implicit reward maximization.
Our decoupling spectrum is distinct from catastrophic forgetting in RL alignment \citep{jin2025rl_panacea}, where models lose pre-trained capabilities across tasks; in our setting, extraction and evidence compete \emph{within} a single task, resembling negative transfer in multi-task learning \citep{ruder2017overview,standley2020tasks,yu2020gradient}, amplified by QLoRA's constrained parameter space \citep{gao2023scaling,moskovitz2024constrained}.
RSFT avoids this intra-task competition by operating on discrete outputs rather than gradients, extending the sample-and-select principle \citep{wang2023selfconsistency} to structured IE with joint quality scoring.

Evidence faithfulness evaluation has received increasing attention: \citet{li2025drift} propose dual-reward inference for faithful rationale generation, and \citet{zhang2024infuse} introduce fine-grained NLI-based faithfulness metrics for summarization.
Our CED scoring builds on similar NLI-based principles but targets evidence-relation entailment rather than free-form rationales.

\citet{zelikman2022star} introduced STaR for iterative self-improvement; \citet{dong2023raft} generalize this with reward-model-based sample filtering; recent analysis shows rejection sampling implicitly performs PPO-like optimization \citep{tang2025rsftppo}.
Our RSFT is a single-round variant applied to evidence-grounded DocRE with CED/NLI scoring as a domain-specific quality filter.
Because RSFT selects complete outputs rather than differentiating through a reward signal, it cannot exploit the extraction-evidence trade-off that gradient methods discover, inherently preserving joint quality.

\begin{abstract}

Large Language Model (LLM) based Document-level Relation Extraction (DocRE) now matches or exceeds encoder baselines in extraction accuracy, yet these methods output bare relation triplets without identifying which sentences support each prediction.
Deployment contexts such as clinical knowledge bases and legal due-diligence systems require verifiable evidence that users can trace to source text.
Encoder-based evidence methods (SAIS, DREEAM) provide supporting sentences but trail LLM approaches in accuracy, leaving a gap between extraction performance and output verifiability.

We formalize evidence-grounded DocRE as a structured generation task and compare Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), and Rejection Sampling Fine-Tuning (RSFT) across three fully evaluated scales (1.7B, 4B, 8B) with 14B validation, two model families, and two datasets.
The na\"{i}ve expectation is that evidence generation always costs extraction accuracy. Our experiments reveal that this cost is not fixed but forms a landscape shaped by capacity, paradigm, and data quality. Within the Qwen3 family, evidence is beneficial at 1.7B ($-$5.63pp Ign-F1) but approximately neutral at $\geq$4B (+0.25$\pm$0.47pp at 4B; positive $=$ cost). Gradient-based optimization amplifies evidence-extraction competition (GRPO catastrophic, DPO gradual), while RSFT with Natural Language Inference (NLI) based scoring avoids decoupling entirely through output filtering rather than gradient pressure.

RSFT compresses training seed variance 4.6--31$\times$ across Qwen3 and LLaMA (complete pairwise seed separation, Cohen's $d{=}2.58$). Our 1.7B RSFT model (51.19 Ign-F1, std 0.09pp) approaches 8B Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) performance (50.19, std 3.23pp) at 4.7$\times$ fewer parameters. Test-set evaluation preserves model ranking across all evaluated scales (Spearman $\rho{=}1.0$).

\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}

Document-level relation extraction (DocRE) requires identifying semantic relations between entity pairs across multiple sentences, a task where encoder-based methods such as \citet{zhou2021atlop} long dominated.
Recent LLM-based approaches have closed this gap: \citet{autore2024} fine-tune LLMs with structured decomposition, \citet{xu2024lmrc} frame it as multi-choice reading comprehension, and \citet{chen2025docksrag} combine retrieval-augmented generation with structured knowledge.
These methods approach or surpass encoder baselines on DocRED \citep{yao2019docred} and Re-DocRED \citep{tan2022redocred} in extraction accuracy, yet every one outputs bare relation triplets $(e_h, r, e_t)$ without indicating \emph{which sentences} support each prediction.
In deployment contexts---clinical knowledge bases, legal due-diligence pipelines, financial compliance systems---users cannot verify a prediction without manually locating its textual basis across a multi-page document.

Encoder-based methods have partially addressed this need: \citet{xiao2022sais} introduce sentence-level evidence supervision as an auxiliary signal, and \citet{ma2023dreeam} extend this with dynamic evidence retrieval through memory attention.
Both produce evidence and improve extraction, but encoder methods now trail LLM-based approaches in accuracy.
The community faces a gap: the most accurate extractors provide no evidence, while evidence-capable methods are no longer competitive.

This gap reflects a structural difference.
In encoder methods, evidence retrieval is classification that regularizes the encoder at negligible cost; in LLM-based DocRE, evidence requires the model to \emph{generate} additional output tokens per triple, increasing output length and decoding complexity.
The na\"{i}ve expectation is that this generation cost always harms extraction accuracy.
Our experiments show this expectation is wrong.
The evidence tax is not a fixed penalty but a landscape shaped by model capacity, optimization paradigm, and training data quality.
Within the Qwen3 family, evidence generation \emph{benefits} extraction at 1.7B ($-$5.63pp Ign-F1, partly through halving output duplication) but is approximately neutral at $\geq$4B (+0.25$\pm$0.47pp at 4B).
Gradient-based optimization amplifies this competition---GRPO collapses extraction under constrained precision, DPO progressively trades extraction for evidence---while discrete sample selection (RSFT) avoids the trade-off entirely by filtering outputs rather than pushing gradients.

We formalize evidence-grounded DocRE as a structured generation task and compare three post-training paradigms---GRPO \citep{shao2024deepseekmath}, DPO \citep{rafailov2023direct}, and RSFT (building on STaR; \citealt{zelikman2022star})---across three fully evaluated scales (1.7B, 4B, 8B) with 14B validation, two model families, and two datasets. Our contributions:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{Evidence generation is not uniformly harmful.} We observe a scale-dependent evidence tax with a within-family capacity threshold: beneficial at 1.7B ($-$5.63pp) but approximately neutral at $\geq$4B (+0.25$\pm$0.47pp at 4B), challenging the assumption that evidence always costs extraction accuracy.

    \item \textbf{Gradient pressure causes evidence-extraction decoupling.} We characterize a decoupling spectrum (GRPO catastrophic $\rightarrow$ DPO gradual $\rightarrow$ RSFT none) and introduce the Evidence-Decoupling Ratio (EDCR) as a diagnostic, validated at per-relation level ($\rho{=}{-}0.79$, $n{=}76$, $p{<}0.001$).

    \item \textbf{RSFT compresses training variance 4.6--31$\times$.} NLI-based sample selection improves mean Ign-F1 across tested scales (+1.2 to +6.6pp); our 1.7B RSFT model (51.19 Ign-F1, std 0.09pp) approaches 8B SFT performance (50.19, std 3.23pp) at 4.7$\times$ fewer parameters, enabling deployment-efficient evidence-grounded extraction.
\end{enumerate}

1	\section{Limitations}
2	
3	Primary development is on the DocRED development set; Re-DocRED test-set evaluation preserves model ranking (Spearman $\rho{=}1.0$) but shows a 18.9--21.9pp absolute drop attributable to higher annotation density (2.82$\times$ more gold triples per document). Exact-match F1 penalizes surface-form-different entity mentions~\citep{wan2024genres}, likely underestimating absolute extraction capability of generative models, though relative comparisons between methods remain valid.
4	
5	We evaluate on two datasets (DocRED, Re-DocRED), both derived from Wikipedia. Cross-domain evaluation is constrained by the absence of evidence-annotated DocRE datasets beyond Wikipedia; this limitation is shared by all prior evidence-aware DocRE work (SAIS, DREEAM, EIDER).
6	
7	We evaluate one algorithm per RL family (GRPO, DPO) with single hyperparameter settings (KL coefficient 0.01, $\beta$ 0.1); other algorithms or settings may produce different decoupling behaviors. CED scoring depends on an external NLI model, and the RSFT ablation uses limited seeds (four for CED, two for flat-NLI). Evidence tax patterns span two model families (Qwen3, LLaMA) but may not generalize to other architectures or scales beyond 14B.
8	
9	EDCR correlates with extraction quality at both method level ($\rho{=}{-}0.89$, $n{=}7$) and per-relation level ($\rho{=}{-}0.79$, $n{=}76$), but has not been validated against human judgments of evidence-extraction alignment. Future work should assess whether EDCR rankings correspond to practitioner assessments of output quality.
10	
11	RSFT improves extraction across scales but evidence quality is unchanged (Evi-F1 $\Delta < 0.4$pp at all scales; Appendix~\ref{sec:error_analysis}). CED-based selection filters for joint quality but does not specifically optimize evidence grounding, suggesting that targeted evidence rewards may be needed to improve evidence quality beyond what data selection achieves.
12	
13	At 1.7B scale, 44.4\% of outputs exhibit repetitive patterns (vs.\ negligible at 4B+); small models may require decoding-time interventions (e.g., repetition penalty) for reliable deployment.

All models are trained on existing annotated data without human subjects involvement. Our evidence-grounding approach aims to improve the verifiability of relation extraction outputs, which supports responsible deployment in high-stakes domains such as clinical and legal information systems by enabling human verification of model predictions. We release code and model outputs to support reproducibility.

\section{Introduction}

Document-level relation extraction (DocRE) requires identifying semantic relations between entity pairs across multiple sentences, a task where encoder-based methods such as \citet{zhou2021atlop} long dominated.
Recent LLM-based approaches have closed this gap: \citet{autore2024} fine-tune LLMs with structured decomposition, \citet{xu2024lmrc} frame it as multi-choice reading comprehension, and \citet{chen2025docksrag} combine retrieval-augmented generation with structured knowledge.
These methods approach or surpass encoder baselines on DocRED \citep{yao2019docred} and Re-DocRED \citep{tan2022redocred} in extraction accuracy, yet every one outputs bare relation triplets $(e_h, r, e_t)$ without indicating \emph{which sentences} support each prediction.
In deployment contexts---clinical knowledge bases, legal due-diligence pipelines, financial compliance systems---users cannot verify a prediction without manually locating its textual basis across a multi-page document.

Encoder-based methods have partially addressed this need: \citet{xiao2022sais} introduce sentence-level evidence supervision as an auxiliary signal, and \citet{ma2023dreeam} extend this with dynamic evidence retrieval through memory attention.
Both produce evidence and improve extraction, but encoder methods now trail LLM-based approaches in accuracy.
The community faces a gap: the most accurate extractors provide no evidence, while evidence-capable methods are no longer competitive.

This gap reflects a structural difference.
In encoder methods, evidence retrieval is classification that regularizes the encoder at negligible cost; in LLM-based DocRE, evidence requires the model to \emph{generate} additional output tokens per triple, increasing output length and decoding complexity.
The na\"{i}ve expectation is that this generation cost always harms extraction accuracy.
Our experiments show this expectation is wrong.
The evidence tax is not a fixed penalty but a landscape shaped by model capacity, optimization paradigm, and training data quality.
Within the Qwen3 family, evidence generation \emph{benefits} extraction at 1.7B ($-$5.63pp Ign-F1, partly through halving output duplication) but is approximately neutral at $\geq$4B (+0.25$\pm$0.47pp at 4B).
Gradient-based optimization amplifies this competition---GRPO collapses extraction under constrained precision, DPO progressively trades extraction for evidence---while discrete sample selection (RSFT) avoids the trade-off entirely by filtering outputs rather than pushing gradients.

We formalize evidence-grounded DocRE as a structured generation task and compare three post-training paradigms---GRPO \citep{shao2024deepseekmath}, DPO \citep{rafailov2023direct}, and RSFT (building on STaR; \citealt{zelikman2022star})---across three fully evaluated scales (1.7B, 4B, 8B) with 14B validation, two model families, and two datasets. Our contributions:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{Evidence generation is not uniformly harmful.} We observe a scale-dependent evidence tax with a within-family capacity threshold: beneficial at 1.7B ($-$5.63pp) but approximately neutral at $\geq$4B (+0.25$\pm$0.47pp at 4B), challenging the assumption that evidence always costs extraction accuracy.

    \item \textbf{Gradient pressure causes evidence-extraction decoupling.} We characterize a decoupling spectrum (GRPO catastrophic $\rightarrow$ DPO gradual $\rightarrow$ RSFT none) and introduce the Evidence-Decoupling Ratio (EDCR) as a diagnostic, validated at per-relation level ($\rho{=}{-}0.79$, $n{=}76$, $p{<}0.001$).

\end{enumerate}

lines: The structural difference between selection and optimization explains why RSFT does not exhibit the decoupling observed in gradient-based methods. GRPO and DPO update model parameters through gradients that optimize a reward signal. When two sub-tasks (extraction and evidence) compete for gradient capacity, the optimizer can discover and exploit the trade-off between them, improving one at the expense of the other. RSFT operates differently: it selects complete outputs and trains on them with standard supervised loss. Because the selection is discrete (accept or reject a full response), there is no gradient pathway through which the model can learn to sacrifice extraction for evidence quality. Only outputs where both extraction and evidence are jointly strong survive the CED filter. This property is not specific to RSFT's design but is a structural consequence of discrete selection over complete outputs: any selection-based method that filters on a joint quality criterion will inherit the same coupling guarantee. The implication for practitioners is direct: when optimizing for multiple coupled generation objectives, selection-based methods preserve inter-objective balance that gradient-based methods disrupt.

\section{Limitations}

Primary development is on the DocRED development set; Re-DocRED test-set evaluation preserves model ranking (Spearman $\rho{=}1.0$) but shows a 18.9--21.9pp absolute drop attributable to higher annotation density (2.82$\times$ more gold triples per document). Exact-match F1 penalizes surface-form-different entity mentions~\citep{wan2024genres}, likely underestimating absolute extraction capability of generative models, though relative comparisons between methods remain valid.

We evaluate on two datasets (DocRED, Re-DocRED), both derived from Wikipedia. Cross-domain evaluation is constrained by the absence of evidence-annotated DocRE datasets beyond Wikipedia; this limitation is shared by all prior evidence-aware DocRE work (SAIS, DREEAM, EIDER).

We evaluate one algorithm per RL family (GRPO, DPO) with single hyperparameter settings (KL coefficient 0.01, $\beta$ 0.1); other algorithms or settings may produce different decoupling behaviors. CED scoring depends on an external NLI model, and the RSFT ablation uses limited seeds (four for CED, two for flat-NLI). Evidence tax patterns span two model families (Qwen3, LLaMA) but may not generalize to other architectures or scales beyond 14B.

EDCR correlates with extraction quality at both method level ($\rho{=}{-}0.89$, $n{=}7$) and per-relation level ($\rho{=}{-}0.79$, $n{=}76$), but has not been validated against human judgments of evidence-extraction alignment. Future work should assess whether EDCR rankings correspond to practitioner assessments of output quality.

RSFT improves extraction across scales but evidence quality is unchanged (Evi-F1 $\Delta < 0.4$pp at all scales; Appendix~\ref{sec:error_analysis}). CED-based selection filters for joint quality but does not specifically optimize evidence grounding, suggesting that targeted evidence rewards may be needed to improve evidence quality beyond what data selection achieves.

At 1.7B scale, 44.4\% of outputs exhibit repetitive patterns (vs.\ negligible at 4B+); small models may require decoding-time interventions (e.g., repetition penalty) for reliable deployment.

\section{Ethics Statement}

This work uses publicly available benchmarks (DocRED, Re-DocRED) derived from Wikipedia, containing no private or sensitive information. All models are trained on existing annotated data without human subjects involvement. Our evidence-grounding approach aims to improve the verifiability of relation extraction outputs, which supports responsible deployment in high-stakes domains such as clinical and legal information systems by enabling human verification of model predictions. We release code and model outputs to support reproducibility.

## Overview

SummaC: Re-Visiting NLI-based Models for Inconsistency Detection in Summarization is a paper published in the Transactions of the Association for Computational Linguistics (TACL) in 2022, volume 10, pages 163-177. The paper is authored by Philippe Laban, Tobias Schnabel, Paul N. Bennett, and Marti A. Hearst.

## Key Problem & Solution

The paper addresses the fact that in the summarization domain, a key requirement for summaries is to be factually consistent with the input document, though previous work had found that natural language inference (NLI) models do not perform competitively when applied to inconsistency detection.

The researchers found that past work suffered from a mismatch in input granularity between NLI datasets (sentence-level), and inconsistency detection (document level). They provide a highly effective and light-weight method called SummaCConv that enables NLI models to be successfully used for this task by segmenting documents into sentence units and aggregating scores between pairs of sentences.

## Benchmark & Results

The paper introduces a new benchmark called SummaC (Summary Consistency) which consists of six large inconsistency detection datasets. On this dataset, SummaCConv obtains state-of-the-art results with a balanced accuracy of 74.4%, a 5% improvement compared with prior work.

## Overview

RelPrior is a novel "Relation as a Prior" paradigm for LLM-based Document-level Relation Extraction (DocRE).

## Key Problem Addressed

LLMs exhibit performance gaps in DocRE requiring fine-grained comprehension, with the commonly adopted "extract entities then predict relations" paradigm leading to gaps because numerous unrelated entity pairs introduce noise.

## Solution Approach

The RelPrior paradigm addresses two main challenges:

1. RelPrior utilizes binary relation as a prior to extract and determine whether two entities are correlated, thereby filtering out irrelevant entity pairs and reducing prediction noise.

2. RelPrior utilizes predefined relation as a prior to match entities for triples extraction instead of directly predicting relation, avoiding misjudgment caused by strict predefined relation labeling.

## Results

Extensive experiments on two benchmarks demonstrate that RelPrior achieves state-of-the-art performance, surpassing existing LLM-based methods.

The paper was posted on arxiv on November 11, 2025.

\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related_work}

Document-level relation extraction (DocRE) requires reasoning across sentence boundaries to identify relations between entity pairs.
DocRED \citep{yao2019docred} established the first large-scale benchmark for this task, catalyzing a line of encoder-based methods that treat DocRE as classification over entity pair representations.
ATLOP \citep{zhou2021atlop} introduced adaptive thresholding for multi-label prediction and localized context pooling for entity representations.
A parallel thread incorporates sentence-level evidence into these architectures.
SAIS \citep{xiao2022sais} introduced evidence supervision as an auxiliary training signal and showed that joint evidence prediction improves extraction through data augmentation and ensemble inference.
DREEAM \citep{ma2023dreeam} extended this approach with dynamic memory-based evidence retrieval that guides attention to supporting sentences.
EIDER \citep{xie2022eider} jointly trains an evidence extractor and fuses evidence representations into the relation classifier.
In all three systems, evidence identification is binary sentence classification over a fixed candidate set, a formulation that adds no output complexity.
Recent work has recast DocRE for large language models.
AutoRE \citep{autore2024} fine-tunes LLMs with QLoRA using a relation-head-facts decomposition; \citet{xu2024lmrc} frame extraction as multi-choice reading comprehension; RelPrior \citep{wang2025relprior} uses relation priors to guide LLM-based extraction; GLiDRE \citep{zhang2025glidre} presents a generalist lightweight approach; Ru-LLM \citep{wang2025rullm} incorporates logical rule constraints; and \citet{chen2025docksrag} combine retrieval-augmented generation with structured knowledge.
These methods match or surpass encoder baselines but produce bare triplets without evidence.
The critical distinction lies in computational nature: in SAIS and DREEAM, evidence retrieval is classification that regularizes the encoder without increasing output length; in LLM-based DocRE, evidence requires additional output tokens per triple, imposing costs that depend on model capacity and optimization strategy.
Whether this cost is inevitable or can be mitigated is the central question of our work.

Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO; \citealt{shao2024deepseekmath}) eliminates the separate value network by computing advantages within groups.
Subsequent work addresses failure modes: DAPO \citep{yu2025dapo} prevents entropy collapse, Dr.\ GRPO \citep{liu2025drgrpo} corrects length bias, and multi-objective variants \citep{liu2026gdpo,ito2025mogrpo} handle competing reward signals.
Applications to structured IE include R1-RE \citep{dai2025r1re} and REAR \citep{wang2025rear}.
Direct Preference Optimization \citep{rafailov2023direct} reformulates RLHF as implicit reward maximization.
Our decoupling spectrum is distinct from catastrophic forgetting in RL alignment \citep{jin2025rl_panacea}, where models lose pre-trained capabilities across tasks; in our setting, extraction and evidence compete \emph{within} a single task, resembling negative transfer in multi-task learning \citep{ruder2017overview,standley2020tasks,yu2020gradient}, amplified by QLoRA's constrained parameter space \citep{gao2023scaling,moskovitz2024constrained}.
RSFT avoids this intra-task competition by operating on discrete outputs rather than gradients, extending the sample-and-select principle \citep{wang2023selfconsistency} to structured IE with joint quality scoring.

Evidence faithfulness evaluation has received increasing attention: \citet{li2025drift} propose dual-reward inference for faithful rationale generation, and \citet{zhang2024infuse} introduce fine-grained NLI-based faithfulness metrics for summarization.
Our CED scoring builds on similar NLI-based principles but targets evidence-relation entailment rather than free-form rationales.

\citet{zelikman2022star} introduced STaR for iterative self-improvement; \citet{dong2023raft} generalize this with reward-model-based sample filtering; recent analysis shows rejection sampling implicitly performs PPO-like optimization \citep{tang2025rsftppo}.
Our RSFT is a single-round variant applied to evidence-grounded DocRE with CED/NLI scoring as a domain-specific quality filter.
Because RSFT selects complete outputs rather than differentiating through a reward signal, it cannot exploit the extraction-evidence trade-off that gradient methods discover, inherently preserving joint quality.
